lesson_title: Rubber Bands, Planks and the Next Plate
hook_text: Raise the price of bread and the till fills. Raise the price of cooldrink and it empties. Why?
clip_script: Some prices you can dodge, and some you cannot. Cooldrink goes up three rand — you switch brands, buy the rival, drink water. Your demand stretched like a rubber band. Bread goes up three rand — you grumble and buy the bread. Your demand is a plank; it barely bends. And here is why every shopkeeper in the country should care: the stretch decides what happens to the till. Raise the price of a plank and the till fills — customers barely leave. Raise the price of a rubber band and the till empties — customers bounce away faster than the higher price pays back. Now step behind a kota stand. The market pays thirty rand a plate, every plate. So interrogate the NEXT plate only: while it costs less than thirty to make, cook it. The moment the next plate costs more than thirty — stop. That stopping rule has a fancy name, marginal revenue equals marginal cost, but it is just a cook counting honestly. One stretch test, one stopping rule — half the year's marks.
visual_style: A price tag pinging off a stretching rubber band, then thudding against a rigid plank; a till filling and emptying as bars rise and fall; a sizzling kota pan with plates sliding out until a cost counter ticks past thirty and a hand stops the pan.
mood: Playful but sharp — street-food economics with real teeth.
pacing: Bouncy alternating beats for rubber band and plank, slowing into the deliberate plate-by-plate count, clean stop on the stopping rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full revision sweep: kitchens, pay packets, till slips and the two drivers of the whole economy.
